title:	gcc -fanalyzer gives up on sst.c and battle.c, and a passing analyze says nothing about it
state:	OPEN
author:	scottdensmore (Scott Densmore)
labels:	
comments:	5
assignees:	
projects:	
milestone:	
issue-type:	
parent:	
sub-issues:	
sub-issues-completed:	
blocked-by:	
blocking:	
number:	171
--
## Problem

The `analyze` test added for #147 runs `gcc -fanalyzer` over the game's
sources with any diagnostic fatal. It buys real coverage over most of
the tree and close to none over the two largest translation units, and
a passing run does not distinguish the two.

GCC abandons paths it finds too complex and reports that only under
`-Wanalyzer-too-complex`, which is off by default. Counted with it on:

| file | bail-outs |
| --- | --- |
| `battle.c` | 169 |
| `setup.c` | 142 |
| `events.c` | 90 |
| `moving.c` | 77 |
| `sst.c` | 46 |
| everything else | 0-6 |

Measured rather than inferred: planting the same uninitialized-read
pattern is **caught** in `setup.c`, `moving.c`, `tuifmt.c`, `events.c`,
`ai.c` and `reports.c`, and **missed** in `sst.c` -- in `main()` and in
the small `cramen()` alike -- and in `battle.c`'s `cloak()`. The
byte-identical snippet in a standalone translation unit is caught, so
it is the size of the surrounding unit and not the snippet.

`battle.c` was confirmed to be compiled at all by planting an unused
variable there, which `-Wunused-variable` duly reported.

## Why it matters

`sst.c` and `battle.c` are where the game's own state machine and its
combat arithmetic live, so they are not the files one would choose to
leave uncovered. Worse, nothing says they are: `analyze` prints
`analyze OK` either way, which is the shape of problem #147 was about
-- a check that reads like coverage and is not, in a place nobody
looks.

The test's comment now records this, so the claim is not stronger than
the truth. That is not the same as closing it.

## Where it was found

By `verifier` on the #147 branch, while checking that the new test
could fail. Filed rather than fixed there: #147 is about the leg
existing at all, and this is about how far it reaches.

## Fixing it

Nothing here is cheap, which is why it is its own issue.

- `--param analyzer-max-enodes-per-program-point=` and its siblings
  raise the ceilings, at a cost in run time that wants measuring
  against the 16s the test takes now.
- Enabling `-Wanalyzer-too-complex` as a *non*-fatal report would at
  least put the number in the output, so a reader can see which files
  were really examined. It cannot be fatal: there are 169 in
  `battle.c` today.
- Splitting the largest functions would help the analyzer and is worth
  doing on its own merits, but it is a refactor of live game code and
  belongs to whatever change has reason to touch them.

Whichever, the honest interim is what the comment now does: say which
files the check actually reaches.

content.content:
What both passes agree on, and what the test's comment now records:

| function | analyzer catches it at defaults |
| --- | --- |
| `setup.c` `newqad()` | yes |
| `battle.c` `phasers()` | yes |
| `sst.c` `cramen()` | no |
| `tui.c` `tui_shutdown()` | no |
| `battle.c` `cloak()` | no |

That table reproduced identically in both passes, so the per-function
finding stands: `battle.c` catches one of its own functions and misses
another, which is what makes the per-file framing in this issue's title
and body wrong regardless of how the parameter question resolves.

What is unsettled is only *why* gcc stops where it does, and whether the
parameter moves it. The test's comment no longer guesses at either, and
says so.

Anyone picking this up should treat the parameter as unmeasured until
someone reproduces one of the two results deliberately -- and should
say which gcc, which value, and where the read was planted, since those
are the three things the two passes could not compare.
--
author:	scottdensmore
association:	owner
edited:	false
status:	none
--
**Settled, and my earlier negative was wrong.** Two later passes
reproduced the recovery; I have now reproduced it too, and found the bug
in my own measurement.

The harness I used planted the probe, compiled, then ran `git checkout`
to restore the file — so every run after the first compiled the
*restored* source. That is why all three parameter values came back
identical: none of them had the probe in the file. A loop that reports
the same answer for every input should have told me that at the time.

Measured properly, gcc 15.2.0, probe at the top of `cloak()`, flags as
the `analyze` test passes them:

| `analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` | `cloak()` |
| --- | --- |
| 5 (default) | missed |
| 6 | missed |
| **7** | **caught** |
| 8 | caught |

So the threshold is exactly 7, two above the default. That makes the
mechanism a budget, as the earlier passes said, and my "cloak() resists
it / complexity is not the whole story" line was simply an artefact.

Two things it does **not** settle:

- **It is not a blanket dial.** `sst.c`'s `cramen()` is still missed at
  8, per the pass that found the threshold. So a single value does not
  buy uniform coverage, and what the right value is — or whether one
  exists — is still the open part of this issue.
- **`-Wanalyzer-too-complex` does not fire here** at any of those
  values, including the ones where the diagnostic is missed. So the
  give-up is still silent, which is the property that makes a passing
  `analyze` read as more than it is. That remains the substance of this
  issue regardless of the parameter.

The test's comment now records the threshold and the `cramen()`
exception, and says raising it is not free: deeper analysis means more
findings of the `newqad()` kind on a check that is `-Werror`. Measuring
that cost tree-wide is the work this issue should carry.
--
author:	scottdensmore
association:	owner
edited:	false
status:	none
--
Two more numbers, both measured on gcc 15.2.0 with the flags the
`analyze` test passes, which between them change what this issue should
ask for.

**The dial does reach `cramen()`, just much further out.**

| function | recovered at `analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` |
| --- | --- |
| `battle.c` `cloak()` | 7 (default is 5; 6 is not enough) |
| `tui.c` `tui_shutdown()` | 8 |
| `sst.c` `cramen()` | **30** — still missed at 12 |

So "not a blanket dial" was the wrong reading of my own earlier data.
There is a value that reaches all three; it is just far above the
default, and the spread between 7 and 30 is itself the interesting part.

**Raising it does not redden the tree.** Over all thirteen sources:

| factor | analyzer diagnostics | wall time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 (default) | 0 | 16s |
| 12 | 0 | 27s |

So the cost of raising it is time, not false positives — at least at 12,
and at least today. That undercuts the reason I gave for leaving it
alone, and it makes the trade worth measuring properly rather than
assumed:

- what the tree reports at 30, where all three functions are reachable,
  and how long that takes;
- how many of any new findings are real, against the `newqad()` kind
  that cost a rewrite or a suppression each under `-Werror`.

If 30 is quiet and the time is tolerable, this issue has a one-line fix
and the uneven-reach problem largely goes away. If it is noisy, the
silent give-up stands as the thing to solve instead — and that part is
unchanged either way: `-Wanalyzer-too-complex` never fires at any of
these values, so nothing in a passing run says a function went
unanalysed.

The test's comment now carries the thresholds, the timings, and the fact
that nothing reddens at 12, so whoever picks this up starts from
measurements rather than from my earlier guesses.
--

#!/bin/sh
# Static analysis over the game's C sources.
#
# This is the check .claude/agents/verifier.md's step 2 asks for. It used
# to ask for cppcheck, clang-tidy or scan-build "if installed", and none
# of the three was installed on the development machine or in CI -- so
# the leg never ran anywhere, the verifier reported the gap honestly on
# every pass, and the gap stayed open. #147.
#
# GCC's own analyzer is what the project actually has: no install, and
# already the compiler CI builds with on Linux. It is a different check
# from the -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes the ci-* presets make
# fatal -- those are what the compiler notices while generating code,
# where this walks paths and tracks what has been written to.
#
# Usage: analyze.sh "<compile flags>" "<compiler>" "<sources;...>"
# Exits 77 (ctest SKIP_RETURN_CODE) where no analyzer-capable compiler
# is available, except on Linux CI, where it fails instead.
#
# Proved to fail two ways, each on a copy of the tree outside the
# repository: a use-after-free planted in sst.c, caught as
# -Werror=use-after-free, and setup.c put back to the form that reads
# an ix only the loop above it sets, caught as
# -Werror=analyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value -- which is the analyzer
# leg specifically, since the plain warning set does not see it.
#
# What it does not prove is how far the analyzer reaches. gcc's reach
# is uneven and it says nothing where it gives up. Measured by planting
# the same uninitialized read in five functions:
# caught in setup.c's newqad() and battle.c's phasers(), missed in
# sst.c's cramen(), tui.c's tui_shutdown() and battle.c's cloak(). So
# it is per function rather than per file -- battle.c catches one of
# its own and misses another -- and a passing run says which files were
# compiled, not which were understood.
#
# Where it stops is a budget. Measured with gcc 15.2.0 against
# --param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor, whose default is 5: cloak()
# comes back at 7 and not at 6, cramen() not until 30. The dial is not
# raised here, and the reason is not that the tree would redden -- at 7
# and at 12 it still reports nothing at all. It is that the cost is
# time, 16 seconds over the sources at the default against 27 at 12,
# and that deeper analysis can surface more findings of the newqad()
# kind, which on a -Werror check cost a rewrite or a suppression each.
# None have appeared yet. #171 has the rest.
#
# An analyzer gone inert is the third case and it does not fail here.
# The canary is the probe below, so a compiler that takes -fanalyzer
# and reports nothing is passed over rather than failing the run: with
# no other candidate the script skips, and on Linux CI that skip is
# itself a failure. Proved by compiling the canary with -fsyntax-only,
# which analyses nothing.
#
# Both of those need ctest to see them properly: exiting 77 is only a
# skip if SKIP_RETURN_CODE says so, and it did not at first -- the
# proofs above ran this script directly and could not see that. Run
# with no analyzer-capable compiler, ctest reports Skipped; with CI=1
# on Linux it reports Failed.

set -u

# The sources live beside this script's parent, and that is how the
# other tests here find what they read.
srcdir=$(unset CDPATH; cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)

# Handed the build's own flags rather than restating them here, which
# is what CMakeLists.txt passes and why. -Werror is added whatever the
# preset says: this test is fatal on a diagnostic even where the build
# it was configured from is not.
flags="${1:-}"
buildcc="${2:-}"
sources="${3:-}"
if [ -z "$flags" ] || [ -z "$sources" ]; then
	echo "usage: analyze.sh \"<flags>\" \"<compiler>\" \"<sources;...>\"" >&2
	exit 2
fi

# A template, and the status checked. Bare `mktemp -d` is a GNU
# extension: BSD mktemp, which is what macOS has, prints usage and
# exits 1. Unchecked that leaves $work empty, every path below absolute,
# the probe unable to write, and the script exiting 77 -- a green macOS

Two passes have now measured `analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` against
`battle.c`'s `cloak()` and got opposite answers. Recording that as a
disagreement rather than picking a side, because I cannot reproduce the
other result even with its own method.

| `int u, k; for (k = 1; k <= skill; k++) u = k; if (u == 42) energy -= 1.0;` | missed | missed | missed |

The second row is the other pass's own probe at its own value, so the
difference is not the pattern and not the parameter as far as I can
reach.

**Theirs**: the same second probe caught at 8, 10, 20 and 100, missed at
5 and 6, planted both at the top of the body and near `battle.c:87`.

says so.

someone reproduces one of the two results deliberately -- and should
say which gcc, which value, and where the read was planted, since those
are the three things the two passes could not compare.

# the probe unable to write, and the script exiting 77 -- a green macOS
# job with nothing analysed, which is the shape of hole #147 is about,
# rebuilt inside the fix for it.
work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/sst-analyze.XXXXXX") || exit 1
[ -n "$work" ] && [ -d "$work" ] || exit 1

# One trap per signal, each exiting. A handler that only cleans up
# returns to where the signal landed, so an interrupted run would carry
# on compiling into a directory it had just deleted and report thirteen
# analysis failures that were nothing of the kind. The one-trap-per-
# signal shape is tests/tui.sh's, though its note beside it is about a
# closed pipe under dash rather than about this.
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 129' HUP
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 130' INT
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 143' TERM
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 141' PIPE

# What a working analyzer has to do, in one file: accept -fanalyzer, and
# actually report on it. The second half is the point -- see the note on
# -fsyntax-only below -- and it is asked of each candidate rather than
# once of the winner, so a compiler that takes the flag and analyses
# nothing is passed over rather than failing the run.
cat > "$work/canary.c" <<'CANARY'
#include <stdlib.h>
int canary(void);
int canary(void) {
	int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
	free(p);
	return *p;			/* use after free */
}
CANARY
[ -s "$work/canary.c" ] || exit 1

# Asking the version string is not enough: macOS ships clang as `gcc`,
# which takes -fanalyzer only as far as an error. Compiling is the
# question worth asking.
#
# Darwin tries only CC and the compiler the build was configured with.
# The runners build with clang but often carry a Homebrew gcc-N, which
# would otherwise be found here and turned loose on the macOS SDK under
# -Werror -- a red job from a Darwin-only warning or an Xcode bump, on
# a check Linux has already delivered. Naming CC, or configuring the
# tree with such a compiler, asks for it there deliberately.
#
# The gcc-N list needs bumping as versions land; without it a machine
# whose only GCC is gcc-16 skips quietly.
candidates="${CC:-} $buildcc gcc gcc-15 gcc-14 gcc-13"
if [ "$(uname -s)" = Darwin ]; then
	# Restricted to CC and the compiler the build was configured
	# with, rather than falling through to any gcc on the path: with
	# CC=clang exported and a Homebrew gcc-N installed, that would
	# find the gcc and turn it loose on the macOS SDK under -Werror.
	# The build's own compiler stays in because a tree configured
	# with GCC on Darwin has already accepted that; AppleClang fails
	# the canary and skips.
	candidates="${CC:-} $buildcc"
fi
cc=""
for candidate in $candidates; do
	command -v "$candidate" >/dev/null 2>&1 || continue
	"$candidate" -fanalyzer -c -o "$work/canary.o" "$work/canary.c" \
	    2>"$work/canary.txt" || true
	if grep -q 'Wanalyzer-use-after-free' "$work/canary.txt"; then
		cc="$candidate"
		break
	fi
done

if [ -z "$cc" ]; then
	# Linux CI builds with GCC, so a skip there would mean the analyzer
	# had gone missing from the one place it is guaranteed. macOS CI
	# builds with clang and is expected to skip.

Correcting two things in the body above, which I wrote from the
`verifier`'s numbers rather than my own and which do not survive being
re-measured.

**"the two largest files" is wrong.** `tui.c` is the largest source in
the target at 1631 lines, against `battle.c` 1518 and `sst.c` 1124.
Whatever governs the blindness, it is not simply size.

**The bail-out table does not explain the misses, and I could not
reproduce it.** `gcc -fanalyzer -Wanalyzer-too-complex` over each source
gives me no "too complex" diagnostics at all, so the 169/142/90/77/46
figures are not something I can stand behind. More to the point, the
table would not support the conclusion even if it held: `setup.c` was
listed at 142 and it is one of the files where the planted read *is*
caught.

**What I did measure**, planting the same uninitialized read in four
functions and compiling with the flags CMake passes the test:

| function | analyzer catches it |
| --- | --- |
| `setup.c` `newqad()` | yes |
| `battle.c` `phasers()` | **yes** |
| `sst.c` `cramen()` | no |
| `tui.c` `tui_shutdown()` | no |

So it is per **function**, not per file: `battle.c` catches one and, per
the original report, misses `cloak()`. `cramen()` is twenty lines long,
which rules out function size as the explanation too.

That makes the issue narrower and stranger than the body says. The
question worth answering is not "which files are too big" but what
actually decides whether the analyzer walks a given function -- and
until that is known, `--param analyzer-max-enodes-per-program-point`
is a guess rather than a fix.

The test's comment now records only the measured table above, and no
longer offers bail-out counts or a size explanation.
--
author:	scottdensmore
association:	owner
edited:	false
status:	none
--
The knob is `--param analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` (default 5), not
`analyzer-max-enodes-per-program-point` as the comment above guessed.
Raising it recovers most of the blindness -- but not all of it, which is
the part worth recording.

Measured, same planted uninitialized read, flags as the `analyze` test
passes them:

| function | default | `analyzer-bb-explosion-factor=40` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sst.c` `cramen()` | missed | **caught** |
| `tui.c` `tui_shutdown()` | missed | **caught** |
| `battle.c` `cloak()` | missed | **still missed** |

So the parameter is the binding one for two of the three, and `cloak()`
resists it. Whatever stops the analyzer there is something else again,
and that is the interesting half: `cloak()` is not especially long, and
`battle.c`'s own `phasers()` is caught at the default.

Also worth noting for anyone reaching for the parameter: no
`-Wanalyzer-too-complex` diagnostic is emitted at either setting, so
there is still nothing in the output to say a function went unanalysed.
That is the property that makes this issue matter more than the depth
itself.

**I would not raise it in the test as it stands.** Deeper analysis means
more findings of the `newqad()` kind -- provable false positives -- on a
check that is `-Werror`, and each one costs either a rewrite of working
game code or a suppression. The trade is worth measuring before taking:
how many new diagnostics appear tree-wide at 40, and how many of them
are real.
--

# Static analysis, which is a different question from the warnings the
# ci-* presets make fatal: those are what the compiler notices while
# generating code, where this walks paths and tracks what has been
# written to. verifier.md's step 2 used to ask for cppcheck, clang-tidy
# or scan-build "if installed" and none of the three was, anywhere, so
# the leg never ran. gcc -fanalyzer is what the project actually has.
# The script skips where no compiler offers it and fails rather than
# skipping on Linux CI, where GCC is the compiler the build already
# uses. Darwin skips by default even where a Homebrew gcc-N is on the
# path: turning that loose on the macOS SDK under -Werror risks a red
# job from a Darwin-only warning, on a check Linux has already
# delivered. Naming CC, or configuring the tree with such a compiler,
# asks for it there deliberately.
#
# Two things the flags below leave out on purpose. CMAKE_C_FLAGS_<CONFIG>
# is not passed, so this analyses unoptimised code in every preset --
# -O3 makes -fanalyzer slower and noisier, and nothing in the tree reads
# NDEBUG, which is the only thing dropping the Release flags would
# otherwise change. And the script adds -Werror whatever SST_WERROR says, so
# `ctest --preset debug` is warning-fatal for this one test where the
# build it was configured from is not. That is deliberate and it is the
# one place this file departs from the policy above: gating on
# SST_WERROR would leave the test with nothing to fail on, since
# deciding which diagnostics count by pattern is what the first version
# tried and got wrong. The cost lands wherever the analyzer differs from
# the one this was written against, older or newer. CI's own gcc is not
# the one it was developed on, so the first run of this test on a pull
# request is the first time the tree meets that analyzer. The same holds
# for a contributor's own gcc, which reddens their ctest rather than CI;
# an ubuntu-latest default bump would redden every pull request and main
# alike, with no local change to blame. Saying at the site why a
# diagnostic is wrong does not clear it -- under -Werror a comment
# silences nothing. Two things do clear it. Restructuring so the
# analyzer can see the invariant is one, and is what #147 did for
# newqad(), which is why that line moved rather than merely gaining a
# comment. A scoped #pragma GCC diagnostic, with the same justification
# beside it, is the other. Widening the gate is neither. #147.
#
# The flags come from here rather than being written out again in the
# script. CMAKE_C_FLAGS already carries the defines, the warning set and
# the -DDEBUG a Debug build adds, and the standard and curses includes
# are the two the build adds separately. Restating any of it in a sixth
# file is how the build recipe drifted before -- see AGENTS.md's note on
# the presets -- and it had already started: the first version of this
# test passed no -std at all, so it analysed as C23 while every preset
# compiled as gnu17.
set(analyze_flags "-std=gnu${CMAKE_C_STANDARD} ${CMAKE_C_FLAGS}")
foreach(dir ${CURSES_INCLUDE_DIRS})
    set(analyze_flags "${analyze_flags} -I${dir}")
endforeach()
# The compiler and the source list come from the build too, for the
# same reason as the flags: a tree configured with a different
# CMAKE_C_COMPILER would otherwise be analysed by whatever gcc the
# script found, and a source added later would go unanalysed with
# nothing to notice. The canary still decides whether the compiler
# named here can analyse at all, so an AppleClang still skips. On
# Darwin only CC and this compiler are tried, never a gcc that merely
# happens to be on the path.
add_test(NAME analyze
         COMMAND ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/analyze.sh
                 "${analyze_flags}" "${CMAKE_C_COMPILER}"
                 "$<TARGET_PROPERTY:sst,SOURCES>")
# SKIP_RETURN_CODE, or the 77 the script exits with where no compiler
# offers -fanalyzer is just a failure -- which is what macOS CI and any
# clang-only machine would have seen.
set_tests_properties(analyze PROPERTIES SKIP_RETURN_CODE 77 TIMEOUT 180)

#!/bin/sh
# Measure the analyze test's cost and noise at a given
# analyzer-bb-explosion-factor. Serial, like the test itself.
#
# usage: sweep.sh <factor> [extra flags...]
set -u
srcdir=/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek
flags="-std=gnu17 -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -DDEBUG -I/usr/include"
sources="sst.c ai.c battle.c events.c finish.c moving.c osx.c planets.c reports.c rules.c setup.c tui.c tuifmt.c"

#!/bin/sh
# Plant an uninitialized read at the top of a named function's body and
# report whether gcc -fanalyzer sees it at a given
# analyzer-bb-explosion-factor.
#
# Regenerates the planted source from a pristine copy every run: the
# harness that got #171's first measurement wrong planted, compiled,
# then `git checkout`-ed, so every run after the first compiled the
# restored file.
#
# usage: probe.sh <file.c> <function-open-line-regex> <factor>
set -u
here=$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd)
tree=$here/probe
flags="-std=gnu17 -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -DDEBUG -I/usr/include"

src=$1
fn=$2
factor=$3

pristine=$here/pristine/$src
[ -f "$pristine" ] || { mkdir -p "$here/pristine"; cp "$tree/$src" "$pristine"; }

probe='{ int sst_probe_u, sst_probe_k; for (sst_probe_k = 1; sst_probe_k <= 2; sst_probe_k++) sst_probe_u = sst_probe_k; { volatile int sst_probe_v = sst_probe_u; (void)sst_probe_v; } }'

awk -v fn="$fn" -v probe="$probe" '
	{ print }
	!done && $0 ~ fn { print probe; done = 1 }
' "$pristine" > "$tree/$src"

# Fail loudly rather than reporting "missed" from an unplanted file.
grep -q sst_probe_u "$tree/$src" || { echo "PLANT FAILED: $src $fn"; exit 2; }

out=$(mktemp)
# shellcheck disable=SC2086
gcc -fanalyzer --param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor="$factor" $flags \
    -c -o /dev/null "$tree/$src" 2>"$out"

if grep -q 'Wanalyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value' "$out"; then
	verdict=caught
elif grep -q 'uninitialized' "$out"; then
	verdict="caught-but-not-by-analyzer: $(grep -o '\[-W[a-z-]*\]' "$out" | sort -u | tr '\n' ' ')"
else
	verdict=missed
fi
printf '%-10s %-22s factor=%-3s %s\n' "$src" "$fn" "$factor" "$verdict"
cp "$pristine" "$tree/$src"
rm -f "$out"

#!/bin/sh
# Static analysis over the game's C sources.
#
# This is the check .claude/agents/verifier.md's step 2 asks for. It used
# to ask for cppcheck, clang-tidy or scan-build "if installed", and none
# of the three was installed on the development machine or in CI -- so
# the leg never ran anywhere, the verifier reported the gap honestly on
# every pass, and the gap stayed open. #147.
#
# GCC's own analyzer is what the project actually has: no install, and
# already the compiler CI builds with on Linux. It is a different check
# from the -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes the ci-* presets make
# fatal -- those are what the compiler notices while generating code,
# where this walks paths and tracks what has been written to.
#
# Usage: analyze.sh "<compile flags>" "<compiler>" "<sources;...>"
# Exits 77 (ctest SKIP_RETURN_CODE) where no analyzer-capable compiler
# is available, except on Linux CI, where it fails instead.
#
# Proved to fail two ways, each on a copy of the tree outside the
# repository: a use-after-free planted in sst.c, caught as
# -Werror=use-after-free, and setup.c put back to the form that reads
# an ix only the loop above it sets, caught as
# -Werror=analyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value -- which is the analyzer
# leg specifically, since the plain warning set does not see it.
#
# What it does not prove is how far the analyzer reaches. gcc's reach
# is uneven and it says nothing where it gives up. Measured by planting
# the same uninitialized read in five functions:
# caught in setup.c's newqad() and battle.c's phasers(), missed in
# sst.c's cramen(), tui.c's tui_shutdown() and battle.c's cloak(). So
# it is per function rather than per file -- battle.c catches one of
# its own and misses another -- and a passing run says which files were
# compiled, not which were understood.
#
# Where it stops is a budget. Measured with gcc 15.2.0 against
# --param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor, whose default is 5: cloak()
# comes back at 7 and not at 6, cramen() not until 30. The dial is not
# raised here, and the reason is not that the tree would redden -- at 7
# and at 12 it still reports nothing at all. It is that the cost is
# time, 16 seconds over the sources at the default against 27 at 12,
# and that deeper analysis can surface more findings of the newqad()
# kind, which on a -Werror check cost a rewrite or a suppression each.
# None have appeared yet. #171 has the rest.
#
# An analyzer gone inert is the third case and it does not fail here.
# The canary is the probe below, so a compiler that takes -fanalyzer
# and reports nothing is passed over rather than failing the run: with
# no other candidate the script skips, and on Linux CI that skip is
# itself a failure. Proved by compiling the canary with -fsyntax-only,
# which analyses nothing.
#
# Both of those need ctest to see them properly: exiting 77 is only a
# skip if SKIP_RETURN_CODE says so, and it did not at first -- the
# proofs above ran this script directly and could not see that. Run
# with no analyzer-capable compiler, ctest reports Skipped; with CI=1
# on Linux it reports Failed.

set -u

# The sources live beside this script's parent, and that is how the
# other tests here find what they read.
srcdir=$(unset CDPATH; cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)

# Handed the build's own flags rather than restating them here, which
# is what CMakeLists.txt passes and why. -Werror is added whatever the
# preset says: this test is fatal on a diagnostic even where the build
# it was configured from is not.
flags="${1:-}"
buildcc="${2:-}"
sources="${3:-}"
if [ -z "$flags" ] || [ -z "$sources" ]; then
	echo "usage: analyze.sh \"<flags>\" \"<compiler>\" \"<sources;...>\"" >&2
	exit 2
fi

# A template, and the status checked. Bare `mktemp -d` is a GNU
# extension: BSD mktemp, which is what macOS has, prints usage and
# exits 1. Unchecked that leaves $work empty, every path below absolute,
# the probe unable to write, and the script exiting 77 -- a green macOS
# job with nothing analysed, which is the shape of hole #147 is about,
# rebuilt inside the fix for it.
work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/sst-analyze.XXXXXX") || exit 1
[ -n "$work" ] && [ -d "$work" ] || exit 1

# One trap per signal, each exiting. A handler that only cleans up
# returns to where the signal landed, so an interrupted run would carry
# on compiling into a directory it had just deleted and report thirteen
# analysis failures that were nothing of the kind. The one-trap-per-
# signal shape is tests/tui.sh's, though its note beside it is about a
# closed pipe under dash rather than about this.
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 129' HUP
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 130' INT
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 143' TERM
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 141' PIPE

# What a working analyzer has to do, in one file: accept -fanalyzer, and
# actually report on it. The second half is the point -- see the note on
# -fsyntax-only below -- and it is asked of each candidate rather than
# once of the winner, so a compiler that takes the flag and analyses
# nothing is passed over rather than failing the run.
cat > "$work/canary.c" <<'CANARY'
#include <stdlib.h>
int canary(void);
int canary(void) {
	int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
	free(p);
	return *p;			/* use after free */
}
CANARY
[ -s "$work/canary.c" ] || exit 1

# Asking the version string is not enough: macOS ships clang as `gcc`,
# which takes -fanalyzer only as far as an error. Compiling is the
# question worth asking.
#
# Darwin tries only CC and the compiler the build was configured with.
# The runners build with clang but often carry a Homebrew gcc-N, which
# would otherwise be found here and turned loose on the macOS SDK under
# -Werror -- a red job from a Darwin-only warning or an Xcode bump, on
# a check Linux has already delivered. Naming CC, or configuring the
# tree with such a compiler, asks for it there deliberately.
#
# The gcc-N list needs bumping as versions land; without it a machine
# whose only GCC is gcc-16 skips quietly.
candidates="${CC:-} $buildcc gcc gcc-15 gcc-14 gcc-13"
if [ "$(uname -s)" = Darwin ]; then
	# Restricted to CC and the compiler the build was configured
	# with, rather than falling through to any gcc on the path: with
	# CC=clang exported and a Homebrew gcc-N installed, that would
	# find the gcc and turn it loose on the macOS SDK under -Werror.
	# The build's own compiler stays in because a tree configured
	# with GCC on Darwin has already accepted that; AppleClang fails
	# the canary and skips.
	candidates="${CC:-} $buildcc"
fi
cc=""
for candidate in $candidates; do
	command -v "$candidate" >/dev/null 2>&1 || continue
	"$candidate" -fanalyzer -c -o "$work/canary.o" "$work/canary.c" \
	    2>"$work/canary.txt" || true
	if grep -q 'Wanalyzer-use-after-free' "$work/canary.txt"; then
		cc="$candidate"
		break
	fi
done

if [ -z "$cc" ]; then
	# Linux CI builds with GCC, so a skip there would mean the analyzer
	# had gone missing from the one place it is guaranteed. macOS CI
	# builds with clang and is expected to skip.
	if [ -n "${CI:-}" ] && [ "$(uname -s)" = Linux ]; then
		echo "FAIL: no compiler with -fanalyzer on Linux CI, so nothing was analysed" >&2
		exit 1
	fi
	echo "SKIP: no compiler whose -fanalyzer reports anything" >&2
	exit 77
fi

# The sst target's own sources, as CMake lists them -- osx.c included,
# and tests/test_tuifmt.c and tests/test_rules.c not, those being test
# harnesses rather than the game. Taken from the build rather than
# globbed here so a source added later cannot go unanalysed quietly.
#
# -Werror, so any diagnostic fails rather than a pattern deciding which
# count. Grepping for -Wanalyzer looked right and was not: a planted
# use-after-free in sst.c came back as plain -Wuse-after-free, which
# -Wall raises before the analyzer gets to it, and the run reported
# clean. The ci-* presets already make -Wall -Wextra fatal, so anything
# new that stops the compile here is either an analyzer finding or
# something those builds would have caught anyway.
# Split the semicolon list CMake passes into positional parameters and
# put IFS back before anything else is expanded -- left set, it splits
# $flags into a single argument and every compile fails on an
# unrecognized option that is the whole flag string.
oldifs=$IFS
IFS=';'
# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # splitting on ';' is the point here
set -- $sources
IFS=$oldifs

status=0
for src in "$@"; do
	case "$src" in /*) ;; *) src="$srcdir/$src" ;; esac
	out="$work/$(basename "$src").txt"
	# shellcheck disable=SC2086  # $flags is a flag list, not one word
	if ! "$cc" -fanalyzer $flags -Werror -c -o "$work/obj.o" "$src" \
	     2>"$out"; then
		echo "FAIL: $(basename "$src") did not analyse clean" >&2
		cat "$out" >&2
		status=1
	fi
done

if [ "$status" -ne 0 ]; then
	exit 1
fi

printf 'analyze OK (%s)\n' "$cc"

#!/bin/sh
# Static analysis over the game's C sources.
#
# This is the check .claude/agents/verifier.md's step 2 asks for. It used
# to ask for cppcheck, clang-tidy or scan-build "if installed", and none
# of the three was installed on the development machine or in CI -- so
# the leg never ran anywhere, the verifier reported the gap honestly on
# every pass, and the gap stayed open. #147.
#
# GCC's own analyzer is what the project actually has: no install, and
# already the compiler CI builds with on Linux. It is a different check
# from the -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes the ci-* presets make
# fatal -- those are what the compiler notices while generating code,
# where this walks paths and tracks what has been written to.
#
# Usage: analyze.sh "<compile flags>" "<compiler>" "<sources;...>"
# Exits 77 (ctest SKIP_RETURN_CODE) where no analyzer-capable compiler
# is available, except on Linux CI, where it fails instead.
#
# Proved to fail two ways, each on a copy of the tree outside the
# repository: a use-after-free planted in sst.c, caught as
# -Werror=use-after-free, and setup.c put back to the form that reads
# an ix only the loop above it sets, caught as
# -Werror=analyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value -- which is the analyzer
# leg specifically, since the plain warning set does not see it.
#
# How far the analyzer reaches is a budget, and at gcc's default it did
# not reach far enough. Measured by planting an uninitialized read only
# -fanalyzer sees -- conditional on a volatile, so -Wall -Wextra at -O0
# says nothing about it -- at the top of five functions and compiling
# with the flags below. At the default it is caught in setup.c's
# newqad() and battle.c's phasers() and missed in sst.c's cramen(),
# tui.c's tui_shutdown() and battle.c's cloak(). Per function rather
# than per file: battle.c catches one of its own and misses another.
#
# --param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor is the dial, default 5, and it
# is raised to 30 below. Each of the three comes back at its own value,
# measured with gcc 15.2.0 by planting the read again at each: cloak()
# at 7 and not at 6, tui_shutdown() at 8, cramen() at 25 and not at 24.
# 30 is the deepest of those with headroom over it, not a value anything
# in the tree needs today.
#
# What raising it costs is time and nothing else so far. Over the
# thirteen sources on this machine: 15s at the default, 32s at 30, 47s
# at 60, with zero diagnostics at every one of them -- and zero under
# the Release configuration's flags too, which analyse different code

# reddens beyond it; it is that no function measured here needs more,

| factor | analyzer diagnostics | wall time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 (default) | 0 | 15s |
| 30 | 0 | 32s |
| 60 | 0 | 47s |

Zero at 30 under the Release configuration's flags too (34s), which
matters because that configuration analyses different code for want of
`-DDEBUG`.

So the condition the last comment set is met: 30 is quiet, and the cost
is time. It is also not a cliff — 60 is quiet as well — which means the
reason to stop somewhere is not that the tree reddens, and a value has
to be argued for rather than found.

## The thresholds, re-measured

The probe is an uninitialized read only the analyzer sees, so a catch is
the analyzer leg and not the plain warning set: `{ volatile int c = 0;
int u; if (c) u = 1; if (u == 42) c = 2; }`. Checked standalone first —
two obvious candidates are not usable, because reading an uninitialized
value *into* a volatile is not flagged at all, and an unconditional read
is flagged by plain `-Wuninitialized` too. Planted at the top of each
function, regenerated from a pristine copy for every single compile.

| function | recovered at |
| --- | --- |
| `battle.c` `cloak()` | 7 (missed at 6) |
| `tui.c` `tui_shutdown()` | 8 |
| `sst.c` `cramen()` | **25** (missed at 24) |

the first value tried above 12, and the cliff is five below it. `newqad()`
and `phasers()` are caught at the default, as before.

| file | too-complex diagnostics |
| --- | --- |
| `battle.c` | 169 |
| `setup.c` | 142 |
| `events.c` | 90 |
| `moving.c` | 77 |
| `sst.c` | 46 |
| `ai.c` | 23 |
| `reports.c` | 6 |
| `tui.c` | 1 |
| `finish.c`, `osx.c`, `planets.c`, `rules.c`, `tuifmt.c` | 0 |

battle.c 169, setup.c 142, events.c 90, moving.c 77, sst.c 46 — the
body's numbers, to the digit. The one difference is `ai.c` at 23, where
the body said "everything else 0-6". They come out as two shapes,
`analysis bailed out early (N enodes)` and `terminating analysis for
this program point`.

gcc -fanalyzer -Wanalyzer-too-complex --param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor=5 \
    -std=gnu17 -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra \
    -Wmissing-prototypes -DDEBUG -I/usr/include -Werror -c -o /dev/null battle.c
```

A guess at where the zero came from, offered as a guess: with `-Werror`
in the flag set every one of these prints as `error:` and not
`warning:`, so a harness grepping for the word `warning` sees none of
them. I counted on the option name instead.

This does not make the visibility half easy. The count *rises* with the
factor rather than falling — `sst.c` goes 46 → 298 at 30, `ai.c` 23 →
188 — because the analyzer explores further before it stops. So it is
not a coverage metric, and at 169 in one file it cannot be made fatal.

strictly more than the nothing this issue assumed was available.

A pull request raises the dial to 30 in `tests/analyze.sh` and nothing
else: 25 is the deepest cliff measured, 30 has headroom over it, and no
function measured here needs more. The script asks the compiler whether
it accepts the `--param` and falls back to the default depth with a note
if not, since a gcc that does not know the option exits on it before
compiling anything and would turn every source into a failure that has
nothing to do with the game. The line a passing run prints now carries
the depth it actually used, so a fallback cannot read as the deeper
check. The `analyze` test's ctest TIMEOUT goes 180 → 300 to keep the
margin it had.

Proved by planting the read in `cramen()` on a copy of the tree outside
the repository and running `tests/analyze.sh` itself: the old script
prints `analyze OK` and exits 0, the new one fails on `sst.c` with
`-Werror=analyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value`.

**Leaving this open**, because the half this does not touch is the one
the comments above identify as the substance: a passing run still says
nothing about where the analyzer gave up, and the counts above show it
gives up in eight of thirteen sources at either depth. The comment in
`tests/analyze.sh` now records those counts and this issue number
against them.

input.content:
Raises `--param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` from gcc's default of 5 to
30 in `tests/analyze.sh`, which is the measurement #171's last comment
asked for and the fix it said would follow if the numbers came out this
way. They did.

## What was wrong

At the default depth the analyzer gives up before reaching several
functions, and gives up silently. An uninitialized read planted at the
top of `sst.c`'s `cramen()`, `tui.c`'s `tui_shutdown()` or `battle.c`'s
`cloak()` is missed, while the same read in `setup.c`'s `newqad()` or
`battle.c`'s `phasers()` is caught — so `analyze OK` covered rather less
than it read as, over the game's own state machine and its combat
arithmetic among others.

## What this does

- Passes `--param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor=30` on every source.
  Measured cliffs, gcc 15.2.0: `cloak()` comes back at 7, `tui_shutdown()`
  at 8, `cramen()` at 25 and not at 24. 30 clears the deepest with room
  over it.
- Asks the compiler whether it takes the option, by recompiling the
  canary with it, and falls back to the default depth with a note if
  not. A gcc that does not know the `--param` exits on it before
  compiling anything, which would turn all thirteen sources into
  failures that have nothing to do with the game — and CI's gcc is not
  the one this was developed against.
- Prints the depth on the line a passing run already printed:
  `analyze OK (/usr/bin/cc, bb-explosion-factor 30)`. A fallback that
  looked identical to the deeper check is the shape of hole #147 was
  about.
- Raises the `analyze` test's ctest `TIMEOUT` from 180 to 300, the run
  having gone from ~15s to ~32s here.

No game source changed.

## Cost, measured

| factor | analyzer diagnostics | wall time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 (default) | 0 | 15s |
| 30 | 0 | 32s |
| 60 | 0 | 47s |

Zero at 30 under the Release configuration's flags too (34s), which
analyse different code for want of `-DDEBUG`. So raising it costs time
and, so far, nothing else: none of the `newqad()`-kind findings that
would each cost a rewrite or a suppression under `-Werror` have appeared.

## Proof it can fail

On a copy of the worktree outside the repository, with an
analyzer-only uninitialized read planted at the top of `cramen()` — the
probe is conditional on a `volatile`, so `-Wall -Wextra` at `-O0` says
nothing about it and a catch is the analyzer leg specifically. The old
`tests/analyze.sh` printed `analyze OK` and exited 0; the new one fails
on `sst.c` with `-Werror=analyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value`. The
fallback leg was proved separately by renaming the `--param` to one no
gcc knows in that same copy: it notes it, reports
`bb-explosion-factor default`, and passes. Both are recorded in the
script's header comment.

## Premise correction on #171

Posted to the issue rather than only here. #171 says in four comments
that `-Wanalyzer-too-complex` never fires. It does: at the default
factor it reports 169 times in `battle.c`, 142 in `setup.c`, 90 in
`events.c`, 77 in `moving.c`, 46 in `sst.c`, 23 in `ai.c`, 6 in
`reports.c`, 1 in `tui.c` and 0 in the remaining five — which is the
table in the issue body that a later comment retracted as
unreproducible, to the digit. A guess at the earlier zero, offered as a
guess: under `-Werror` these print as `error:` rather than `warning:`.

It does not change what this pull request does, and it does not make the
visibility half cheap: the counts *rise* with the factor (`sst.c` 46 →
298 at 30) because the analyzer explores further before it stops, so
they are not a coverage metric, and at 169 in one file the warning
cannot be made fatal. It does mean the give-up is reportable, where the
issue assumed nothing was available. The script's comment now carries
those counts.

**#171 stays open** for that half, which this does not touch.

## Workflow

- `ui-review` **not run**: no game source changed, and the only altered
  output is a test script's own pass line and a ctest timeout. Nothing
  here reaches a player. `code-review` was told so when invoked.
- Issues filed: none new. What was found belongs to #171 and went on
  #171, per step 9's "if it is already filed, add what you learned".

AGENTS.md step 4 asks for a mutation proof. The proof itself can be
blind, in ways that look exactly like a result.

Three that actually happened here:

- **Wrong layer.** Proofs that ran `tests/analyze.sh` directly could
  never see that ctest lacked `SKIP_RETURN_CODE 77`, so the skip path
  was a failure on every clang-only machine. If a test is wired into
  ctest, prove it *through* ctest.
- **A harness that undoes the break.** A loop that planted a probe,
  compiled, then ran `git checkout` tested unmodified source on every
  run after the first. It reported the same answer for all inputs —
  which is the tell.
- **A pattern-matching assertion.** Grepping the analyzer output for
  `-Wanalyzer` missed a planted use-after-free that `-Wall` reported
  first as plain `-Wuse-after-free`. Making every diagnostic fatal is
  robust where deciding which ones count by pattern is not.

**Why:** a green mutation run means one of two things — the test is
blind, or the break was. Ruling out the second is the whole value of
the exercise, and it is the half that gets skipped.

**How to apply:** before believing a mutation result, say out loud what
would have to be true for the break to reach the code under test, and
check that one thing. When two runs disagree, suspect the harness
before the subject — see [[agent-defs-snapshot-at-spawn]] for the other
case where the thing under test was not the thing being run.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Raises `--param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` from gcc's default of 5 to
30 in `tests/analyze.sh`, which is the measurement #171's last comment
asked for and the fix it said would follow if the numbers came out this
way. They did.

## What was wrong

At the default depth the analyzer gives up before reaching several
functions, and gives up silently. An uninitialized read planted at the
top of `sst.c`'s `cramen()`, `tui.c`'s `tui_shutdown()` or `battle.c`'s
`cloak()` is missed, while the same read in `setup.c`'s `newqad()` or
`battle.c`'s `phasers()` is caught — so `analyze OK` covered rather less
than it read as, over the game's own state machine and its combat
arithmetic among others.

## What this does

- Passes `--param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor=30` on every source.
  Measured cliffs, gcc 15.2.0: `cloak()` comes back at 7, `tui_shutdown()`
  at 8, `cramen()` at 25 and not at 24. 30 clears the deepest with room
  over it.
- Asks the compiler whether it takes the option, by recompiling the
  canary with it, and falls back to the default depth with a note if
  not. A gcc that does not know the `--param` exits on it before
  compiling anything, which would turn all thirteen sources into
  failures that have nothing to do with the game — and CI's gcc is not
  the one this was developed against.
- Prints the depth on the line a passing run already printed:
  `analyze OK (/usr/bin/cc, bb-explosion-factor 30)`. A fallback that
  looked identical to the deeper check is the shape of hole #147 was
  about.
- Raises the `analyze` test's ctest `TIMEOUT` from 180 to 300, the run
  having gone from ~15s to ~32s here.

No game source changed.

## Cost, measured

| factor | analyzer diagnostics | wall time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 (default) | 0 | 15s |
| 30 | 0 | 32s |
| 60 | 0 | 47s |

Zero at 30 under the Release configuration's flags too (34s), which
analyse different code for want of `-DDEBUG`. So raising it costs time
and, so far, nothing else: none of the `newqad()`-kind findings that
would each cost a rewrite or a suppression under `-Werror` have appeared.

## Proof it can fail

On a copy of the worktree outside the repository, with an
analyzer-only uninitialized read planted at the top of `cramen()` — the
probe is conditional on a `volatile`, so `-Wall -Wextra` at `-O0` says
nothing about it and a catch is the analyzer leg specifically. The old
`tests/analyze.sh` printed `analyze OK` and exited 0; the new one fails
on `sst.c` with `-Werror=analyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value`. The
fallback leg was proved separately by renaming the `--param` to one no
gcc knows in that same copy: it notes it, reports
`bb-explosion-factor default`, and passes. Both are recorded in the
script's header comment.

## Premise correction on #171

Posted to the issue rather than only here. #171 says in four comments
that `-Wanalyzer-too-complex` never fires. It does: at the default
factor it reports 169 times in `battle.c`, 142 in `setup.c`, 90 in
`events.c`, 77 in `moving.c`, 46 in `sst.c`, 23 in `ai.c`, 6 in
`reports.c`, 1 in `tui.c` and 0 in the remaining five — which is the
table in the issue body that a later comment retracted as
unreproducible, to the digit. A guess at the earlier zero, offered as a
guess: under `-Werror` these print as `error:` rather than `warning:`.

It does not change what this pull request does, and it does not make the
visibility half cheap: the counts *rise* with the factor (`sst.c` 46 →
298 at 30) because the analyzer explores further before it stops, so
they are not a coverage metric, and at 169 in one file the warning
cannot be made fatal. It does mean the give-up is reportable, where the
issue assumed nothing was available. The script's comment now carries
those counts.

**#171 stays open** for that half, which this does not touch.

## Workflow

- `ui-review` **not run**: no game source changed, and the only altered
  output is a test script's own pass line and a ctest timeout. Nothing
  here reaches a player. `code-review` was told so when invoked.
- Issues filed: none new. What was found belongs to #171 and went on
  #171, per step 9's "if it is already filed, add what you learned".

Raises `--param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` from gcc's default of 5 to
30 in `tests/analyze.sh`, which is the measurement #171's last comment
asked for and the fix it said would follow if the numbers came out this
way. They did.

## What was wrong

At the default depth the analyzer gives up before reaching several
functions, and gives up silently. An uninitialized read planted at the
top of `sst.c`'s `cramen()`, `tui.c`'s `tui_shutdown()` or `battle.c`'s
`cloak()` is missed, while the same read in `setup.c`'s `newqad()` or
`battle.c`'s `phasers()` is caught — so `analyze OK` covered rather less
than it read as, over the game's own state machine and its combat
arithmetic among others.

## What this does

- Passes `--param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor=30` on every source.
  Measured cliffs, gcc 15.2.0: `cloak()` comes back at 7, `tui_shutdown()`
  at 8, `cramen()` at 25 and not at 24. 30 clears the deepest with room
  over it.
- Asks the compiler whether it takes the option, by recompiling the
  canary with it, and falls back to the default depth with a note if
  not. A gcc that does not know the `--param` exits on it before
  compiling anything, which would turn all thirteen sources into
  failures that have nothing to do with the game — and CI's gcc is not
  the one this was developed against.
- On Linux CI that fallback is a failure instead, mirroring the gate
  the script already had for finding no analyzer-capable compiler
  there. Falling back silently would be this check reverting to exactly
  the reach it exists to fix, and ctest prints nothing for a passing
  test, so the note would reach no log anyone reads.
- Prints the depth on the line a passing run already printed:
  `analyze OK (/usr/bin/cc, bb-explosion-factor 30)`. A fallback that
  looked identical to the deeper check is the shape of hole #147 was
  about.
- Raises the `analyze` test's ctest `TIMEOUT` from 180 to 300, the run
  having gone from ~15s to ~32s here.

No game source changed.

## Cost, measured

| factor | analyzer diagnostics | wall time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 (default) | 0 | 15s |
| 30 | 0 | 32s |
| 60 | 0 | 47s |

Zero at 30 under the Release configuration's flags too (34s), which
analyse different code for want of `-DDEBUG`. So raising it costs time
and, so far, nothing else: none of the `newqad()`-kind findings that
would each cost a rewrite or a suppression under `-Werror` have appeared.

## Proof it can fail

On a copy of the worktree outside the repository, with an
analyzer-only uninitialized read planted at the top of `cramen()` — the
probe is conditional on a `volatile`, so `-Wall -Wextra` at `-O0` says
nothing about it and a catch is the analyzer leg specifically. The old
`tests/analyze.sh` printed `analyze OK` and exited 0; the new one fails
on `sst.c` with `-Werror=analyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value`. The
fallback leg was proved separately with a shim on the path that forwards
to gcc but rejects that `--param` the way a gcc too old for it would: it
notes the fallback, reports `bb-explosion-factor default` and passes,
and with `CI=1` exits 1 on the new gate instead. All three are recorded
in the script's header comment.

The cliffs above belong to that exact planted read and not to the
functions — `verifier` planted a shorter one in `cramen()` and got 10
rather than 25, because what is planted decides how much budget is left
to walk the rest. What holds whichever is used is the two ends: missed
at 5, caught at 30. The comment says so and gives the statement it
measured, so the boundary is reproducible rather than merely asserted.

## Premise correction on #171

Posted to the issue rather than only here. #171 says in four comments
that `-Wanalyzer-too-complex` never fires. It does: at the default
factor it reports 169 times in `battle.c`, 142 in `setup.c`, 90 in
`events.c`, 77 in `moving.c`, 46 in `sst.c`, 23 in `ai.c`, 6 in
`reports.c`, 1 in `tui.c` and 0 in the remaining five — which is the
table in the issue body that a later comment retracted as
unreproducible, to the digit. A guess at the earlier zero, offered as a
guess: under `-Werror` these print as `error:` rather than `warning:`.

It does not change what this pull request does, and it does not make the
visibility half cheap: the counts *rise* with the factor (`sst.c` 46 →
298 at 30) because the analyzer explores further before it stops, so
they are not a coverage metric, and at 169 in one file the warning
cannot be made fatal. It does mean the give-up is reportable, where the
issue assumed nothing was available. The script's comment now carries
those counts.

## Workflow

  output is a test script's own pass line and a ctest timeout. Nothing
  here reaches a player. `code-review` was told so when invoked.
- Issues filed: none new. What was found belongs to #171 and went on
  #171, per step 9's "if it is already filed, add what you learned".

```
gcc (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0
analyze OK (/usr/bin/cc, bb-explosion-factor 30)
analyze.sh exit=0 after 33s
```

I also ran the 13-source loop at factor 30 under **both** flag strings CMake passes (Debug with `-DDEBUG`, Release without) on that gcc 13.3: **zero diagnostics**, 30s and 32s. So CI will not redden either from a rejected param or from new findings on a compiler two majors older than the one the comment was measured against. Bracketing: gcc 13.3 clean and gcc 15.2.0 clean (the local ctest runs) — gcc 14 untested, which is the only version a future `ubuntu-latest` bump could land on that nobody has looked at.

Timeout headroom is ample: CI's runner is comparable-to-slightly-faster than this machine on this suite (`tui` 155.85s there vs 174.37s here; `eof` 18.96 vs 19.26), and factor 30 costs 30–33s here, against `TIMEOUT 300` and a job currently finishing in 5m53s of a 15-minute budget.

The 3x gap is on the analyzer leg specifically. It does not change the verdict (every measurement is far inside the timeout), but it means the cost and reach numbers in the comment may not predict CI's; the comment already scopes them to "this machine", so I am not raising it as a claim to fix.

## Re-verification of the three items

The silent-fallback hole is genuinely closed.
2. **The 25/24 cliff.** Reproduced exactly, on a copy of the working tree outside the repository with the comment's literal statement planted at the top of `cramen()`: gcc 15.2.0 gives 0 diagnostics at 5, 0 at **24**, 2 at **25**, 2 at 30. - `tournamen.trk` sits in the repository root (Aug 16, gitignored since 91fbe91). Pre-existing, not from this diff.

## What ran

Working tree state: branch `test/analyze-explosion-factor` has **no commits ahead of `main`**; the change is entirely unstaged (`M CMakeLists.txt`, `M tests/analyze.sh`), nothing staged or untracked, no game source touched. Nothing in the repository was modified by this pass.

- `cmake --preset ci-debug && cmake --build --preset ci-debug --clean-first` — exit 0, zero warnings/errors.
- `cmake --preset ci-release && cmake --build --preset ci-release --clean-first` — exit 0, zero warnings/errors.
- `ctest --preset ci-debug` — 12/12 passed, 357.24s (`tui` 174.37s, `analyze` 32.27s).
- `ctest --preset ci-release` — 12/12 passed, 350.06s (`tui` 171.61s, `analyze` 30.80s).
- `shellcheck -s sh tests/analyze.sh` — clean.
- Depth/gate probes described above (docker `ubuntu:24.04` + `gcc:13`, shim compiler, planted-read copy under `/tmp/claude-1000/.../scratchpad/copy`).
- Journeys: `printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nstatus\nlrscan\nquit\ny\n'` piped to `build/ci-debug/sst` and `build/ci-release/sst` — exit 0 both, 77 lines each, no carriage returns, clean sign-off. TUI journeys covered by the `tui` test in both configurations.

**On scope, since you asked me to say rather than run out of duty:** I ran the full battery, but honestly, only part of it could have been affected. No game source, build flag or preset changed, so `golden`, `tournament`, `eof`, `help`, `tui`, `journey*`, `tuifmt`, `rules` and `score` were controls, not tests of this delta. The delta's own coverage is: both `ci-*` builds, `ctest -R '^analyze$'` in both configurations, and the gate/depth probes above. I ran the rest anyway because it costs wall time rather than context and gives you a green baseline for the commit — but a narrower rerun of just those would have been defensible, and is what I would run again if only the comment text changed.</result>

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Raises `--param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` from gcc's default of 5 to
30 in `tests/analyze.sh`, which is the measurement #171's last comment
asked for and the fix it said would follow if the numbers came out this
way. They did.

## What was wrong

At the default depth the analyzer gives up before reaching several
functions, and gives up silently. An uninitialized read planted at the
top of `sst.c`'s `cramen()`, `tui.c`'s `tui_shutdown()` or `battle.c`'s
`cloak()` is missed, while the same read in `setup.c`'s `newqad()` or
`battle.c`'s `phasers()` is caught — so `analyze OK` covered rather less
than it read as, over the game's own state machine and its combat
arithmetic among others.

## What this does

- Passes `--param=analyzer-bb-explosion-factor=30` on every source.
  Measured cliffs, gcc 15.2.0: `cloak()` comes back at 7, `tui_shutdown()`
  at 8, `cramen()` at 25 and not at 24. 30 clears the deepest with room
  over it.
- Asks the compiler whether it takes the option, by recompiling the
  canary with it, and falls back to the default depth with a note if
  not. A gcc that does not know the `--param` exits on it before
  compiling anything, which would turn all thirteen sources into
  failures that have nothing to do with the game — and CI's gcc is not
  the one this was developed against.
- On Linux CI that fallback is a failure instead, mirroring the gate
  the script already had for finding no analyzer-capable compiler
  there. Falling back silently would be this check reverting to exactly
  the reach it exists to fix, and ctest prints nothing for a passing
  test, so the note would reach no log anyone reads.
- Prints the depth on the line a passing run already printed:
  `analyze OK (/usr/bin/cc, bb-explosion-factor 30)`. A fallback that
  looked identical to the deeper check is the shape of hole #147 was
  about.
- Raises the `analyze` test's ctest `TIMEOUT` from 180 to 300, the run
  having gone from ~15s to ~32s here.

No game source changed.

## Cost, measured

| factor | analyzer diagnostics | wall time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 (default) | 0 | 15s |
| 30 | 0 | 32s |
| 60 | 0 | 47s |

Zero at 30 under the Release configuration's flags too (34s), which
analyse different code for want of `-DDEBUG`. So raising it costs time
and, so far, nothing else: none of the `newqad()`-kind findings that
would each cost a rewrite or a suppression under `-Werror` have appeared.

## Proof it can fail

On a copy of the worktree outside the repository, with an
analyzer-only uninitialized read planted at the top of `cramen()` — the
probe is conditional on a `volatile`, so `-Wall -Wextra` at `-O0` says
nothing about it and a catch is the analyzer leg specifically. The old
`tests/analyze.sh` printed `analyze OK` and exited 0; the new one fails
on `sst.c` with `-Werror=analyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value`. The
fallback leg was proved separately with a shim on the path that forwards
to gcc but rejects that `--param` the way a gcc too old for it would: it
notes the fallback, reports `bb-explosion-factor default` and passes,
and with `CI=1` exits 1 on the new gate instead. All three are recorded
in the script's header comment.

The cliffs above belong to that exact planted read and not to the
functions — `verifier` planted a shorter one in `cramen()` and got 10
rather than 25, because what is planted decides how much budget is left
to walk the rest. What holds whichever is used is the two ends: missed
at 5, caught at 30. The comment says so and gives the statement it
measured, so the boundary is reproducible rather than merely asserted.

## Premise correction on #171

Posted to the issue rather than only here. #171 says in four comments
that `-Wanalyzer-too-complex` never fires. It does: at the default
factor it reports 169 times in `battle.c`, 142 in `setup.c`, 90 in
`events.c`, 77 in `moving.c`, 46 in `sst.c`, 23 in `ai.c`, 6 in
`reports.c`, 1 in `tui.c` and 0 in the remaining five — which is the
table in the issue body that a later comment retracted as
unreproducible, to the digit. A guess at the earlier zero, offered as a
guess: under `-Werror` these print as `error:` rather than `warning:`.

It does not change what this pull request does, and it does not make the
visibility half cheap: the counts *rise* with the factor (`sst.c` 46 →
298 at 30) because the analyzer explores further before it stops, so
they are not a coverage metric, and at 169 in one file the warning
cannot be made fatal. It does mean the give-up is reportable, where the
issue assumed nothing was available. The script's comment now carries
those counts.

**#171 stays open** for that half, which this does not touch.

## Workflow

- `ui-review` **not run**: no game source changed, and the only altered
  output is a test script's own pass line and a ctest timeout. Nothing
  here reaches a player, and the change alters nothing about what gets
  compiled into the binary. `code-review` was told so when invoked.
- `verifier` findings, all three fixed rather than resolved by argument:
  the Linux-CI gate above was its coverage finding; the probe text in
  the comment answers its "25/24 is probe-dependent and not
  reproducible from the comment"; and `CMakeLists.txt` now says 16s, so
  180/16 → eleven and 300/32 → nine both close.
- Issues filed: none new. What was found belongs to #171 and went on
  #171, per step 9's "if it is already filed, add what you learned".

would each cost a rewrite or a suppression under `-Werror` have appeared.
